title: Spicy Sauteed Fish
description:
More and more, we’ve tried to have seafood on our menus at home. And, this has become a whole lot easier with you girls out of the house – you never seemed to like the smell of fish at home. But, your – and our – tastes change, and we all seem to enjoy seafood more these days.
Of course, tasty preparations make having fish (or anything) that much more fun. This recipe we got several years back from Bon Appétit. Not only does it have some of our favorite ingredients – tomatoes, black olives, and garlic – but it is very easy to make (and doesn’t smell or taste fishy!)
According to the article, this is an “efficient” dish to make, since it’s got all kinds of the things that are good for you, it’s low in fat, and it can be made quickly. They also recommended making this with some cut up sweet potatoes (with chopped fresh thyme and minced garlic, roasted at 450 degrees for 30 to 40 minutes).
ingredients: 2 pounds tilapia, red snapper, or orange roughy fillets
½ teaspoon dried crushed red pepper
1 cup Kalamata olives or other brine-cured black olives, or green olives, chopped
Heat olive oil in heavy large skillet over medium-high heat.
directions: Sprinkle fish with salt and pepper. Add half of fish to skillet and sauté until just opaque in center, about 3 minutes per side. Transfer fish to platter. Repeat with remaining fish.
Add some anchovies and capers to this fish dish and you have a “puttanesca” sauce, with a spicier flavor and more pungent aroma, often served with spaghetti.

According to one story, the name comes from the fact that the intense fragrance of this sauce was like a siren’s call to the men who were on the evening prowl for the voluptuous Italian “ladies of pleasure.”
No matter, it’s very good and it’s great fun to say “puttanesca,” as if you were fluent in Italian.
Add parsley and crushed red pepper to same skillet; sauté 1 minute.
Add tomatoes, olives, and garlic; sauté until tomatoes are soft and juicy, about 2 minutes.
Season sauce with salt and pepper; spoon over fish.
